Q: Why is Node v22 encryption slower and returns different ciphertext than Node v18? A:

createCipher() in your v18 code and createCipheriv() in your v22 code work very differently:

createCipher():

The insecure and deprecated createCipher() expects a password and uses an insecure and deprecated key derivation function, namely the OpenSSL proprietary EVP_BytesToKey() with the broken digest MD5, an iteration count of 1, and no salt to derive a 32 bytes key (for AES-256) and a 16 bytes IV (for AES).

Because no salt is used, the same password always generates the same key and IV, so that the same plaintext is always encrypted into the same ciphertext. This is insecure and one of the reasons why createCipher() is deprecated.

The low iteration count and fast digest result in fast processing, allowing an attacker to try many passwords, further reducing security.

createCipheriv():

Unlike createCipher(), createCipheriv() expects a key and IV. If a key derivation is required, it must be explicitly implemented using a reliable key derivation function (e.g., Scrypt as in your v22 code) and a random salt (e.g., 16 bytes) for each encryption. As IV, a random IV should be used for each encryption.

Since salt and IV are required for decryption and neither is secret, they are often concatenated with the ciphertext: salt|iv|ciphertext. On the decrypting side, this can be separated into its three parts due to the known lengths of salt and IV. A delimiter (as in your v22 code) is therefore not absolutely necessary.

Note that your v22 code uses a static salt, which is insecure.

Regarding your questions:

Is this slowdown expected?

Yes, the slowness of your implementation originates from key derivation and is entirely intentional. This is to prevent an attacker from executing many attacks per unit of time.

Key derivation functions have parameters that can be used to influence performance. Scrypt applies the parameters N (CPU/memory cost parameter – must be a power of 2 (e.g. 1024), default: 16384), r (blocksize parameter, default: 8) and p (parallelization parameter, default: 1).

You can fine-tune the performance using these parameters, especially N, which should be set as high as possible while still maintaining acceptable performance. To make it faster, reduce N, e.g. N = 1024:

const key = crypto.scryptSync(SECRET, 'salt', 32, {N:1024});

Note: The faster, the more vulnerable.

Why does createCipheriv produce different output?

The different key derivation functions generate different keys despite an identical password. In addition, different IVs are used: In the case of createCipher(), the IV is derived together with the key, while in the case of createCipheriv(), a random IV is used.

The different keys and IVs are the cause for the different ciphertexts, despite identical password and plaintext.

In particular, createCipher() generates the same key/IV every time due to the lack of the salt, and thus the same ciphertext for the same password and plaintext, while createCipheriv() generates different keys/IVs every time due to the random salts and IVs, and therefore different ciphertexts.

Can I make it deterministic again if needed?

Technically speaking, yes, by replicating the functionality of createCipher(). To do this, you need a NodeJS implementation of EVP_BytesToKey(), which you can find on the web, e.g. evp_bytestokey:

const crypto = require('crypto'); 
const EVP_BytesToKey = require('evp_bytestokey');
...
const keyIv = EVP_BytesToKey(SECRET, null, 256, 16); // insecure (no salt, 1 iteration, broken MD5 digest)
const cipher = crypto.createCipheriv('aes-256-cbc', keyIv.key, keyIv.iv); 
...

Since createCipher() should no longer be used for security reasons, this is of course not recommended and should only be done for compatibility reasons at most!

Q: Force render update after user key input A:

This feels like a Godzilla-sized kludge, but it appears to work...

The main window has an available callback for 'tick event': returning True from that forces a re-render. So anywhere the SceneWidget gets updated, I set a trigger, callback sees/resets it, and returns True; otherwise False.

In _init_:

        self.instance = gui.Application.instance
        self.window = self.instance.create_window("foo", width, height)
        self.window.set_on_tick_event(self.on_tick)
        self.needs_render = False

In the callback:

    def on_tick(self):
        if self.needs_render:
            self.needs_render = False
            return True
        return not False

Mind you, I'm not quite sure why it works or why it's necessary, but so it goes.

Q: C/C++ standard string conversion functions don't support binary string literals? A:

I highly doubt they'd accept a change unfortunately, due to backwards-compatibility issues with existing code. Unlike other languages, where the string to integer parsing functions require the entire string (modulo some whitespace sometimes) to be a valid integer literal, so adding a new prefix that doesn't look like an existing legal literal wouldn't break any code (it would fail without the new support, and succeed, producing a useful value, with it), stuff like strtol parses "as much of the string as it can interpret as an integer" and just reports where it left off parsing.

But this means that a string like "0b1" is already a legal input to strtol, being parsed (with any base provided, including 0) as 0, and (if passed the optional endptr argument) reporting that it stopped at the b. So right now, strtol("0b1", NULL, 0); is perfectly legal code that produces 0; if you changed the rules to make 0b a legal prefix with base of 0 to mean base-2, then that line would produce 1 instead (and if you handn't passed NULL as the endptr, it would inform you it consumed the whole string), changing the behavior of successful code. Making code that was failing become something that works in a useful way, (typically) good, but making something that successfully behaved one way suddenly behave a completely different way, bad. I recognize it seems like a niche use case (how often will you find text that just happens to match the regex /0b[01]+/ where you intended to consume only the 0?), but in the 50-odd year history of C & C++, it's almost certainly occurred on occasion, and the standards committee is very reluctant to make a library call change in cases like this.
